<reason>Side B won by making the debate easier to decide. B's core dilemma — a ban either big enough to matter (attracting reuse math and substitution effects) or small enough to be safe (capturing none of the promised collection/litter/drain savings) — was never fully broken. A's honest concession that no pre-ban measured example could be named, and the surviving concrete case of an "unnecessary outer bag," let B argue persuasively that the middle ground was empty and that the opening's cost story had shrunk to its skeleton. B also answered A's best symmetry pressure (why can officials revise fees but not phaseouts?) with the original sunk-cost/constituency asymmetry: a wrong fee fails cheaply while a wrong ban survives on political momentum. A had real strengths — the targeted-scope definition from the opening, the point that pricing requires the same accounting regulators supposedly cannot do, the fee dilemma in the closing (either it produces the same transition costs or it fails to secure the endpoint), and clean epistemic discipline in refusing to invent an example. But A never landed a decisive blow on the dilemma itself, and the proportionality response ("a narrow rule need only justify its own costs") conceded rather than reclaimed the territory B contested. B's progression, weighing, and exploitation of the live clash were consistently sharper, though B's occasional overreach ("the actual state of every ban on the books") keeps this clear rather than dominant.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was B's Rebuttal 2 and Closing, which converted A's A1 concession ("I cannot name a specific pre-ban measurement") into the argument that every conditional in A's case rides on a comparison never performed, and that the only concrete example offered — the outer bag — recovers essentially none of the public costs A's opening promised, leaving B's trivial-or-dangerous dilemma standing as the frame for the final decision.</best_rebuttal>
